Heeey, man. Sorry I didn't respond for so long, work, y'know. Anyway. Survival tips.

Overhead, overhead, overhead. Overhead. I said it alot because it's important. You need to factor in every ongoing cost you're going to incur for at least a month of operability. (Not including labour, of course, cause that'll be you anyway.) That is the minimum goal your business has to reach to be sustainable. Your first month is going to be the most expensive, because you're going to have to outfit the building, bring it up to code, and buy all your ingredients.

Straight up, your food margins aren't going to be very big at all and there's really nothing you can do about that. If you get a panini press, you might be able to charge a little more but it's not going to be terribly rewarding either way. Saw fries, good idea for sandwiches, but fryers are expensive and cleaning intensive. Plus you have to pay for oil removal, unless you find somebody making diesel fuel out of it, who'll take it for free. You're going to make your money in drinks. Figure $5 for a medium whatever and work out what it costs you to make it and see if you're survivable. You're going to have to judge for yourself if you're location will provide the needed traffic.

You're going to need a gimmick of some sort, anyway, which is also going to be dependant on your tastes and location. I would say try to cater to the more refined crowd, make sure you stock some exotic coffees. Me, for example, when I hear about a place that has good, authentic, Turkish coffee, that's what I'm getting. It's delicious, but it's finicky to make and therefore expensive.

Uhh, let's see what else... somebody said WiFi, yeah, of course you have to offer that. Who said kratum, wtf, not in a coffee shop. Lots of other good ideas, though, I hope you do well. Give out a Voater discount code? ;P

Lemme know if you've got anything else, I'll see what I know about it.

Don't. Random coffee shops are virtually impossible to get to a sustainable level of business. It helps that you already have the brick and mortar, but that doesn't mean that cost is zero.

There's a great blog floating around the net about a mid-30s professional couple who gave up their good paying careers to start a funky coffee shop. They started up with high ideals and a French pastry chef who made croissants that were so light they practically floated, but as it turned out every time they sold one they lost a couple bucks. And then there were the patrons who'd get a single cup and take up a table or booth for 1/2 the day, using the free wifi (don't even think about not having free wifi). Eventually they had to lay everyone off to cut costs so they could keep the lights on. The couple worked everyday, all day and grew to hate each other, themselves, and most especially coffee.

Or something like that.

Down the street from where I worked was a well known doughnut/coffee chain. They did a roaring business but the company was poorly managed and went tits up. It was a fantastic location though and someone had the great idea to buy the shop and re-open it with a similar sounding name but otherwise keep the colors and branding from the predecessor. The coffee and food was pretty much the same as well. It didn't even last a year. Go figure. It's a Tim Hortons now and the cars line up across the parking lot every morning for the drivethru.

So either buy a franchise or do something else with it, but don't waste your time, money, and effort on a coffee shop.
Write up a business plan, get a business loan, and do it. As for how to do the first step, find a friend with a business degree, or research it yourself via the Internet or via business school.

It was touched a little bit by GoddammitMrNoodle... but be prepared to work. A lot. Even if you're successful and don't shut down (as Memorexem said) be prepared to work your GD ass off for the first couple of years.

Then, crunch the numbers, do the math and business plan (as said before) ... it's an uphill battle, but it's not impossible!
